newsitem.title: UK: Europe grains uncompetitive, despite high dollar.
newsitem.headline: Europe grains uncompetitive, despite high dollar.

text.p: A strong dollar was a move in the right direction for European grains this week, but was not enough to make them competitive in the short term, traders said.
Harvesting dominated thinking as market players awaited news on quality. But variable weather slowed progress in places.

Thursday's EU tender award of 170,000 tonnes of wheat at a tax of 0.50 Ecus did nothing to improve the market's tone. Most traders thought it utterly neutral, although it was judged negative by the London futures market, reflecting a UK hope for a more generous EU approach. The tender award values early September soft wheat at around $145.15 per tonne, according to Reuters calculations.
French traders complained their wheat exports were not competitive in the short term, traders said. But they did think it looked better for November onwards.
The management committee decision to put a 0.50 Ecu tax on wheat exported under the daily system was surprisingly friendly and would allow some exporters to cover themselves, French traders said.
Overall traders reported little activity on the French domestic market. Good progress was made with the harvest late last week and early this, and traders were assessing the state of the crop.

Britain's grain market remained unusually quiet for the time of year, traders said. The variable weather meant farmers did not feel under any great pressure to sell and at current prices did not want to. "There's a certain resistance and resentment from farmers to accept current spot prices," one trader said.
"At the moment it doesn't feel like a normal harvest," he said. The bulk of barley harvesting has been done in southern areas, but only around half in the midlands and further north.
Yields were disappointing compared with last year's good levels, while quality looked highly variable.
Although wheat harvesting has started, less than one per cent has been done, the trader reckoned.
"The trade's guessing when we are going to see some action from the farmer," he said. "There isn't a great deal of demand for UK wheat, but then we're not getting much from the farms," he said.
Frustration at the lack of farmer selling drove some buyers into the futures market later in the week and helped mitigate the effects of sterling strength and disappointment at the EU tender result.
German grain traders said the EU's free market export tender on Thursday had been neutral.

Sellers would have preferred a continuation of the "nil value" entry in the daily system instead of the 0.5 Ecus/tonne tax but they were pleased with the 170,000 tonnes of wheat authorised for export.
Wheat prices in the coming weeks would depend on harvest qualities across Europe, they said.

Germany's wheat harvest will start in a fortnight and prices were rising because buyers in the export trade appeared to be betting on lower qualities in other European crops and on eastern European demand from flood-hit regions.
If prices continued to rise, this could soon raise concern among domestic millers.
The EU could have been more generous with barley rebates because prices were at risk of falling even further due to domestic consumption problems, traders also said.
Barley demand from the Dutch feed industry was down and German ex-farm prices for new crop of 195-210 marks were 20 marks down from last year. The fob price for July/Aug was 245.

Spanish milling wheat was scarcely available with dealers predicting more imports due to poor quality. Barley prices fell as the harvest started to trickle through, while maize was lower, with forecasts for a bigger than initially expected harvest this year.
An official forecast for this year's maize crop was upped to 4.33 million tonnes in June from an estimated 4.15 million in May.

Italian durum prices rose over the week because of lack of availability. The Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies (Ismea) noted that part of the the rise could be attributed to price increases in other European centres.
Soft wheat and maize prices were unchanged from the previous week and the Italian market was getting ready to close for summer holidays.
